name: PT Kimia Farma Tbk

frontmatter.title: Kimia Farma: the state pharma restructuring, priced as an option
frontmatter.summary: We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp206 (-41.2%). The 2026 operating recovery is real but is consumed by interest, so profit before tax only turns positive in FY2031 in our base case. Fair value is the operating business plus non-operating property, weighted across a bear case that wipes out the equity and a bull case that requires flawless execution; the market already pays more than that expected value.
thesis: The operating turnaround is genuine — nine-month operating profit rose IDR227.0bn and EBITDA reached IDR503.0bn — but interest of roughly IDR481.5bn a year absorbs it, and we do not see positive pre-tax profit before FY2031 [S3, S4].

The enterprise is worth less than its debt: our DCF puts enterprise value at IDR5,287.0bn against net debt of IDR6,601.7bn at 31 December 2025, so the equity's value comes from IDR1,175.3bn of investment properties, a halved IDR339.1bn of assets held for sale and a negative minority balance, not from the pharmacy chain [S3].

The cut in the nine-month net loss is misleading in two ways: IDR590.1bn of FY2025 finance cost is not the run-rate, and the loss attributable to the parent was IDR-62.0bn, with a positive IDR49.1bn earned by minorities, while a large slice of first-nine-month interest was accrued but not paid in cash [S3, S4].

The market pays 11.9x our FY2027E EBITDA for a business that still does not cover its interest, which is a bet on the Danantara separation and a state-led recapitalisation rather than on the current earnings stream [S0, S7].

The shares are not investable at size for most mandates: free float is 10.2% against the exchange minimum and three-month turnover IDR1.1bn, so the Rp206 target is a valuation statement, not a liquidity call [S0, S9, S25].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Kimia Farma Tbk at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp206, against a last price of Rp350, a total return of -41.2% [S0]. The target is the probability-weighted value of our three scenarios after a liquidity discount. Our base case values the shares at Rp28, the bull case at Rp1,412, and the bear case leaves the equity worthless because enterprise value falls below net debt. The weights are 60.0%, 15.0% and 25.0% respectively, and the weighted value before the discount is Rp228 [S0].

The company is the manufacturing, distribution and retail arm of Indonesia's state pharmaceutical holding. Manufacturing sells to third parties, distribution runs the KFTD network that supplies pharmacies, hospitals and government institutions, and retail operates the Kimia Farma pharmacy chain with its clinic and laboratory network [S2]. Revenue of IDR9,223.3bn in FY2025 split into distribution at IDR4,329.2bn, retail at IDR3,360.7bn, manufacturing at IDR729.5bn and other activities. The group is controlled by PT Bio Farma with 89.8% of the shares and a single Series A Dwiwarna share, leaving a free float of 10.2% [S9].

Our variant view is that the market reads the 2026 numbers as the start of an earnings recovery, while we read them as an operating recovery that the capital structure consumes. Nine-month operating profit rose to IDR227.0bn and EBITDA to IDR503.0bn, but the loss attributable to the owners of the parent was IDR-62.0bn against a group figure of IDR13.0bn because minorities earned IDR49.1bn [S3, S4]. Part of the improvement is a bank-restructuring gain sitting in finance income, cash interest paid was IDR139.3bn against IDR357.7bn of accrued finance cost, and the group still pays roughly IDR481.5bn of finance costs a year against an EBIT line that only reaches IDR449.3bn by FY2030 [S3]. In our base case pre-tax profit turns positive in FY2031, and only just.

The consequence is that the equity is a leveraged call on the balance sheet rather than a claim on a profitable business. Our DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR5,287.0bn, below net debt of IDR6,601.7bn at 31 December 2025, virtually unchanged at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the engine carries, so the operating business contributes little to equity value in the base case [S0]. What the shareholder owns is IDR1,175.3bn of investment properties carried at fair value, IDR339.1bn of non-current assets held for sale, and a negative non-controlling-interest balance of IDR-100.9bn that adds to rather than subtracts from equity [S3]. The base value, Rp28, is therefore a property-and-minority arithmetic, not an earnings valuation.

Three things move the value. First, the interest line: the 2026 restructuring moved long-term bank loans to IDR6,232.4bn and extended maturities, and every hundred basis points on a debt stack of that size is worth more to the equity than any plausible margin gain [S3]. Second, the imported-cost line: more than 95.0% of raw materials are imported, mainly from India and China, so the rupiah and API prices drive gross margin more than price increases do [S9]. Third, the state's intentions: the Danantara plan to separate KAEF from the Bio Farma holding is the single event that could convert the bull case into the base case, and it has no timetable [S7].

We are not recommending the shares at Rp350. The base case is Rp28, the bear case is a total loss of equity, and the probability-weighted value of Rp206 is well below the market price: the convexity that a deeply levered equity offers is already paid for, and more than paid for, at today's level. An investor who wants the Danantara option should wait for a price that reflects the odds, and the thin float means most institutional mandates cannot build a position in it in any case [S0]. The Danantara separation, a state capital injection or a property sale could each change this arithmetic, but none is modelled in any scenario because none has an announced size, price or date; they are unquantified optionality, not base-case value.

Kimia Farma is one of the oldest industrial names in the Indonesian pharmaceutical sector and today operates as an integrated group across three linked businesses: manufacturing active and finished doses, distributing medicines through its own logistics arm, and dispensing them through the largest state-owned pharmacy chain. The annual report presents four reporting segments. Distribution is the largest at IDR4,329.2bn of external sales in FY2025, retail is second at IDR3,360.7bn, manufacturing contributes IDR729.5bn and the remaining activities, which include the laboratory and clinic businesses, make up the balance of IDR9,223.3bn [S2].

The distribution arm, KFTD, is the part of the group with genuine scale economics. It serves hospitals, pharmacies, government institutions and other outlets across the archipelago, and the company's own public expose puts the reach at 16,988 pharmacies alone, alongside a hospital and government-institution client base [S9]. That network is the reason a manufacturer would want to own KAEF: it is a route to market that a new entrant cannot replicate quickly, and it is the asset the state has been unwilling to let fail. It is also the segment with the thinnest margins, because distribution economics are a function of volume and working capital rather than brand.

Retail is the segment that has done most damage. The pharmacy chain, at 1,050 outlets at end-2025, was cut back from a larger footprint as leases were exited, and the retail line fell sharply in FY2025 while the group as a whole was shrinking [S2]. The clinic and laboratory businesses sit alongside the pharmacies and are small enough that the annual report folds them into the other segment. Retail is where the group meets consumers directly, and where the 2025 rationalisation of the product portfolio — 181 products discontinued, leaving 494 — was most visible on the shelf [S7].

Manufacturing is small as a share of group revenue but strategically important. It supplies the group's own labels, increasingly sells to third parties, and is the part of the business the state cares about for import substitution. The group employs 9,838 people, a large share on contract terms, and the 2025-2026 programme has centralised procurement and cut headcount cost to bring the operating-expense ratio down from the level the company quotes as its starting point towards a target of 29.0% [S9]. That target is an entity-level measure and is more ambitious than the consolidated ratio the group reports.

The controlling shareholder is PT Bio Farma, the state pharmaceutical holding, which holds 89.8% of the shares and one Series A Dwiwarna share carrying special rights [S9]. The remaining free float of 10.2% makes this a policy asset with a listed minority rather than a genuinely public company. The most important structural fact about the business today is that Danantara, the state investment vehicle, intends to separate KAEF from the Bio Farma holding as part of a plan to cut the number of state-owned enterprises, and management has said it is waiting for direction from Bio Farma rather than driving the process itself [S7].

Kimia Farma's history runs back to the colonial state pharmacy monopoly, which is why its brand carries recognition far beyond its current market share and why its property estate includes assets in central Jakarta and other prime locations that are unrelated to pharmaceutical production. The group was listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange as part of the state's privatisation programme and has been part of the state pharmaceutical holding since that structure was created. None of this history is load-bearing for the valuation, but it explains the mismatch between a small operating profit and a large book value.

The Indonesian pharmaceutical market is large, structurally under-penetrated relative to GDP and heavily prescription-driven. Prescription products account for 67.7% of the market and over-the-counter products for 32.3%, which matters for KAEF because its manufacturing and distribution arms earn most of their money on prescription volumes channelled through hospitals and clinics, while the retail chain is where the over-the-counter business lives [S2]. Domestic manufacturers hold 80.7% of the overall market, so the competitive field is local even though the inputs are not.

Growth has been solid. The Ministry of Industry targeted growth of 6.6% for the chemical, pharmaceutical and traditional-medicine sector in 2025, IQVIA projected growth of up to 10.0% a year, and the Coordinating Ministry for the Economy reported that the sector grew 8.1% in Q3-2026, driven by new chemical investment and by pharmaceutical capacity expansion aimed at the national health-insurance programme [S2, S8]. A market growing at that rate with a company shrinking is a share-loss story, and that is what FY2025 was: group sales fell while the market grew [S2].

The demand driver that matters most is the national health insurer, BPJS Kesehatan, and the JKN programme behind it. The government is explicitly steering pharmaceutical expansion towards drugs usable in the BPJS programme, and the e-catalogue procurement system sets prices for a large part of the volume flowing through hospitals and primary care [S8]. For a distributor and manufacturer of generic and branded-generic products, that means volume is available but price is administered. The companies that earn good returns in this system have the lowest cost of goods and the strongest brands in the private market; KAEF has neither in full measure.

The second structural fact is import dependence. More than 95.0% of pharmaceutical raw materials are imported, mainly from India and China, so the sector's gross margin is a function of the rupiah and of global API prices as much as of domestic pricing power [S9]. This is the most important external influence on our forecasts. It is also why we do not extrapolate the 2026 gross-margin improvement indefinitely: the improvement came from product mix and procurement, but the input cost base remains dollarised while a large part of revenue is rupiah-priced and, in the BPJS channel, price-capped. Our base case holds the rupiah flat at spot and therefore excludes the macro deck's USD/IDR path, which is above spot for FY2027E [S0]; the model has no FX variable, so the effect of a depreciation reaches the P&L only through the gross-margin sensitivity, whose lower rows show what a two-point cost squeeze does to the value. We state this as a limitation rather than hide it: a rupiah at the deck's FY2027E rate would raise imported API cost on more than 95.0% of raw materials and is not in the base.

Competition is intense. The annual report counts 2,043 pharmaceutical manufacturers in the country, and the listed peer set includes large branded players with double-digit operating margins alongside smaller generic manufacturers whose margins are closer to KAEF's [S2]. KAEF's position is best described as a national champion by mandate rather than by economics: it has distribution reach and a state-backed balance sheet, but not the pricing power of the branded multinationals or the cost position of the largest domestic manufacturer. Its manufacturing share is small, its retail chain is sub-scale against the modern-format pharmacy chains, and its distribution arm competes with private logistics operators that do not carry a pharmacy chain's fixed costs.

Five-forces view. Buyer power is very high: the government, through BPJS and the e-catalogue, is the largest single buyer and sets prices administratively, while private hospitals and pharmacy chains negotiate hard. Supplier power is high for active ingredients, where the group is a price-taker on imported inputs, and low for packaging and logistics. Rivalry is high and rising, with thousands of manufacturers and a consolidating retail channel. The threat of new entrants is moderate in manufacturing, where regulation and capital requirements are real, and high in retail, where a private chain can open stores faster than KAEF can. Substitutes are a slow force: generics substitute for branded products and the government encourages that substitution, which caps branded pricing [S2, S8, S9].

The moat, such as it is, sits in distribution and in the licence to operate as a state-owned supplier to the public system. Neither is a pricing moat; both are volume and access moats. That is consistent with the financial history in section three: the group can generate revenue of roughly IDR9,223.3bn but converted that into an operating loss in the most recent audited year [S2]. Our terminal assumptions therefore do not credit the group with a durable margin above the mid-single digits, and the section four valuation shows what happens to the equity when the margin stays there.

The five-year record is one of a business that grew sales, lost control of costs and then lost sales. Revenue ran from IDR9,232.7bn in FY2022 to a peak in FY2024 and back to IDR9,223.3bn in FY2025, so the top line is roughly flat over the period while the operating result collapsed from IDR466.6bn to IDR-79.8bn [S2]. The net result followed: a loss of IDR-2,260.7bn in FY2023, IDR-1,208.2bn in FY2024 and IDR-443.4bn in FY2025, of which IDR-335.0bn was attributable to the owners of the parent and the remainder to minorities [S2, S3].

The cost structure explains most of it. Gross margin was 33.2% in FY2025 and operating expenses consumed more than the gross profit, which is why the operating line was negative. Nine-month 2026 numbers show the correction: a gross margin of 35.3% on our full-year estimate and an operating profit of IDR227.0bn, with the company reporting EBITDA growth above thirty per cent [S3, S4]. We model FY2026E revenue of IDR9,375.5bn, an operating profit of IDR199.7bn and a net loss of IDR-145.0bn, deliberately below the nine-month run-rate because the fourth quarter has historically carried year-end true-ups that depress both gross margin and the operating line [S2].

Two adjustments to reported data drive our numbers. First, depreciation and amortisation. The data pack's D&A line is materially below the audited segment note; we cannot print the pack figure because the pack has no archived text, but the LK governs and its segment note reconciles FY2025 D&A to IDR488.1bn and nine-month 2026 D&A to IDR324.9bn [S3]. We use the LK figure, which is the one that lowers EBITDA and deepens the reported operating loss relative to the pack. Second, equity and minorities. The pack's parent equity omits the transaction-with-NCI component the LK carries, and its minority balance is a positive asset where the LK shows a negative liability; both are corrected in our balance sheet, so equity attributable to owners is IDR2,885.7bn and minority interest is IDR-100.9bn [F10, F27, F28] [S3]. Parent-attributable profit is likewise not the group figure: nine-month 2026 shows IDR-62.0bn to the parent and a positive IDR49.1bn to minorities, and the group loss of IDR13.0bn is their sum [S3].

The balance sheet is the heart of the investment case. Gross debt is IDR6,978.8bn against cash of IDR377.1bn, so net debt is IDR6,601.7bn at 31 December 2025 and net debt to FY2025 EBITDA is 16.2x [S0]. Finance costs were IDR590.1bn in FY2025, and IDR121.8bn of nine-month 2026 finance income was a restructuring gain rather than interest earned, so recurring interest income is small [S3]. The 2026 restructuring extended maturities and moved long-term bank loans to IDR6,232.4bn, and the group also carries state shareholder loans, of which IDR246.4bn is short-term [S3]. None of this reduces the debt; it buys time.

Our forecast keeps the balance sheet physical rather than assuming a deleveraging the cash flow cannot support. Interest near the FY2025 level against an operating profit of a few hundred billion rupiah means free cash flow to equity is negative through the forecast, so net borrowing rises modestly in FY2026 and is flat thereafter, leaving debt near its current level and the interest line near IDR481.5bn [S3]. Equity attributable to owners therefore falls from IDR2,885.7bn to a trough before the cumulative profits of the later years rebuild it, and pre-tax profit turns positive in FY2031 at IDR1.4bn [S0].

Cash generation is adequate at the operating line and inadequate after capital spending and interest. Free cash flow to the firm is IDR163.6bn in FY2025 and IDR92.2bn in our FY2026 estimate; we normalise capital expenditure to IDR187.5bn in FY2026 and about 4.0% of sales by FY2030, because the distressed actual of 1.4% of sales in FY2025 is not a maintenance level for a group with an asset base this large [S2, S3]. Working capital is assumed at 4.5% of sales, consistent with the nine-month position, and the dividend stays at zero because retained earnings remain in deficit and the last distribution predates the current losses [S3].

Earnings quality. The headline improvement in 2026 is partly optical. The nine-month group net loss of IDR13.0bn compares with a far larger loss a year earlier, but the parent's share was IDR-62.0bn and minorities contributed IDR49.1bn, so the parent is further from break-even than the group number suggests [S3]. Part of the improvement is a bank-restructuring gain sitting in finance income: total finance income of IDR140.6bn is mostly that gain rather than recurring interest [S3]. Cash conversion is weak: net cash from operations was IDR9.9bn, a small fraction of EBITDA, and cash interest paid of IDR139.3bn against IDR357.7bn accrued means the operating cash line is being held up by IDR357.7bn of interest that has not been paid [S3]. The negative minority balance means subsidiary losses are absorbed outside the parent's equity, which flatters the parent's book value relative to the economics, and that credit reverses as soon as minorities are profitable again; the FY2025 opinion is unqualified but struck on a going-concern basis that depends on state support [S2, S3]. We classify these as optics-class flags, not manipulation-class: the disclosures are there, the restructuring gain is separately identified, and the auditor signed without qualification — but the interest forbearance is the one that could become a solvency flag.

We value KAEF on a discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm, and we give that method the whole weight. The reasons are arithmetic rather than doctrinal. The group has negative earnings in the recent past and in our forecast years, so there is no meaningful price-to-earnings multiple to strike. The enterprise-value-to-EBITDA cross-check on trailing EBITDA uses FY2025 as the LTM year, when EBITDA of IDR408.3bn was a cyclical trough; applying a peer multiple to a trough year produces an equity value so far below zero that the engine floors it, and a floored leg silently subtracts value from the target for no economic reason [S0, S2]. We therefore report the multiples as cross-checks and let the DCF set the target, with the reasoning disclosed rather than buried in a weighting.

The cost of capital is built from the house inputs and pinned inside the house IDR band. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, giving a cost of equity on an unlevered beta of 0.70 that relevers to 1.79 at market gearing of 2.0. CAPM alone gives a WACC below the house band because two-thirds of the capital is state-supported debt; we therefore add a 2.0% company-specific premium to the cost of equity for state dependence, the thin float and negative free cash flow to equity through FY2030. The pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC is 9.4%, the marginal CAPM rate of the risk-free rate plus the corporate spread in the macro deck [S0], which is above the 6.9% embedded rate the group actually pays on its grandfathered book [S3] — a deliberately conservative choice, and the reason the discount rate sits at the bottom rather than the middle of the band. The result is a weighted average cost of capital of 11.5%, with equity at 33.3% and debt at 66.7% after tax at 22.0%. Reconciling a 19.8% cost of equity with a 11.5% WACC takes one line of arithmetic: the equity is only a third of the capital, and the debt costs 9.4% before tax. That is a high hurdle for a business whose operating margin is in the low single digits, and it is the correct hurdle; at a higher WACC the base value falls further and the rating does not improve, as the sensitivity table below shows through its WACC axis.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR5,287.0bn, with 51.9% of that value in the terminal period. That is the disclosure that matters most in this valuation: half the enterprise value is a perpetuity, not a forecast. Terminal growth of 4.0% is below long-run nominal GDP because a distributor that has lost share for three years does not deserve the market's growth rate. The multiple-survival test fails it: capitalising terminal-year EBITDA of IDR1,147.4bn at the implied terminal value produces an exit multiple above the multiple today's enterprise value implies on the same EBITDA, which is multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume rather than a fade to the cost of capital. The terminal margin of 8.6% is above anything in the audited record, and terminal return on new capital only clears the 11.5% hurdle if capex stays at the 4.0%-of-sales level we model while the asset base depreciates faster than it is replaced — a shrinking business earning a normal return, not a franchise earning excess returns. Subtracting net debt — IDR6,601.7bn at 31 December 2025 and almost the same at the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the engine uses — leaves a negative operating equity value, and adding the IDR1,175.3bn of investment properties, half of the IDR339.1bn of assets held for sale and the negative minority of IDR-100.9bn produces an equity value of Rp23 per share today, rolled forward to Rp28 at the valuation date [S3].

The bridge is the only reason the base value is positive, so it needs its own warning. The operating business contributes negative equity — an enterprise value of IDR5,287.0bn against net debt measured at 30 September 2026, the pack's gross debt less cash of IDR467.6bn at that date, which is almost identical to the IDR6,601.7bn of 31 December 2025 — and the two non-operating assets are what turn that negative into a positive Rp28: between them they are worth more than the entire base equity value. We take the investment properties of IDR1,175.3bn at their full carrying value but the IDR339.1bn of non-current assets held for sale at only half, because the disposal has been pending since December 2025, no binding sale had been announced by our valuation date, and a stalled sale is the base rate for this asset [S3, S7]. We could not source which group entity holds the investment properties, so no minority deduction is made; if they sit in Kimia Farma Apotek (majority-owned) or Phapros, the parent's share of any realisation is smaller than the balance sheet line, which is a further downside not in the number. Rental income is not separately disclosed and sits at most in the other-income line inside EBIT, so the double count, if any, is small against the asset, and property fair-value gains go through OCI and never touch EBIT. The negative minority balance of IDR-100.9bn is retained because the LK's parent equity is presented that way, but it is not cash: it reverses as minorities earn profits again, as the nine-month 2026 result already shows [S3]. The 10.0% liquidity discount is applied to the probability-weighted value, not to the base case: Rp228 times one minus the discount gives the Rp206 target, while the base case of Rp28 and the bull case of Rp1,412 are undiscounted. The rating does not depend on that construction: even with the bull weight raised to about a quarter, the weighted and discounted value stays below the market price.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative. On our FY2027E EBITDA the market is paying 11.9x, roughly twice the peer median the engine applies, and on book value the shares trade at 0.7x, on a book that already includes revalued property [S0]. A price-to-book below one is not cheap when the book earns a negative return on equity of -12.9%; it is the market marking the asset base down towards what a buyer would pay for the property and the distribution licence alone. The multiple the market is really paying is a multiple on a recovery that has not happened, and our DCF says that recovery, at the margin we model, is worth less than the debt.

Sensitivity is asymmetric. A percentage point on the terminal margin moves equity value by more than a percentage point on the discount rate, because the equity is a thin residual on a large enterprise value, and a half-point change in the interest cost has an effect of similar magnitude through the cash flow available to shareholders. The table shows the grid; the practical implication is that equity value is a function of two variables we do not control, the state's willingness to refinance and the rupiah.

What the price implies. At Rp350 the market capitalisation is IDR1,948.3bn and enterprise value is that plus net debt, which requires a revenue growth rate of 9.5% in FY2027E to justify the price on our own model — above anything the group has delivered in the audited series and well above our base case. That is not impossible — it is roughly what the bull case assumes — but it requires the Danantara separation, a lower interest bill and a gross margin that survives an imported-cost shock, all at once. Our probability-weighted value, Rp228 before the liquidity discount and Rp206 after it, says the market is paying well above the expected value of that option rather than a discount to it.

The first risk is refinancing, and it is the largest. Net debt is IDR6,601.7bn at 31 December 2025 and finance costs are roughly IDR481.5bn a year, against an operating profit that only reaches IDR449.3bn in FY2030 in our base case [S3]. The 2026 restructuring moved maturities out and long-term bank loans to IDR6,232.4bn, and the state has demonstrated a willingness to lend through shareholder facilities, of which IDR246.4bn is short-term [S3, S5]. The recovery is also being carried by unpaid interest: nine-month 2026 finance cost was IDR357.7bn but cash interest paid was only IDR139.3bn, so the balance accrues to the lenders — principally the banks, which account for almost all of the finance cost, with the state shareholder loan supplying the rest [S3]. That forbearance is a live trigger, not a footnote. Our bear case assumes it ends and the accrued interest is settled in cash, which starves the working capital the recovery needs; a lender that stops rolling, or a state that converts its support into equity at a discount, changes the per-share arithmetic immediately. Likelihood: medium over the forecast period; impact: high, because the equity is the residual.

The second risk is the exchange rate and imported input costs. With more than 95.0% of raw materials imported, a rupiah depreciation or an API price shock compresses gross margin faster than the company can reprice, because the BPJS channel is price-administered [S9]. This is the mirror of the bull case and the reason we keep gross margin in the mid-thirties rather than extrapolating the 2026 improvement. Likelihood: high over any five-year window; impact: medium to high depending on the size of the move.

The third risk is regulatory and political. Pharmaceutical pricing, the e-catalogue, local-content rules and the national health insurer's budget all set the terms on which KAEF earns revenue, and a new pricing rule can reset the economics of a product line overnight [S8]. The Danantara restructuring adds a second layer: separation from the Bio Farma holding could bring capital and focus, or leave the group without the holding's balance sheet at exactly the wrong moment [S7]. Likelihood: high that some policy change lands; impact: uncertain in direction, which is why it sits in both the bull and the bear case.

The fourth risk is operational execution and disclosure. The group has missed its own plans for three years, the fourth quarter has repeatedly produced true-ups that reverse the trend of the first nine months, and the reported segment data has required restatement against the data pack [S2, S3]. A repeat of a large fourth-quarter write-down would invalidate our FY2026 estimate and, more importantly, the credibility of the recovery narrative. Likelihood: medium; impact: medium on the model, high on sentiment.

The fifth risk is liquidity and ownership. Free float is 10.2% against the exchange minimum, with a compliance deadline at the end of March 2029; the house registry records the company as not compliant, and the gap is the central thesis risk rather than a footnote. Closing it means the state selling down several percentage points of the register — hundreds of millions of shares, which at three-month average daily turnover of IDR1.1bn is many months of trading rather than a block trade — and the alternative to a sell-down is the delisting path the exchange uses for persistent non-compliance [S0]. Three-month average daily turnover is IDR1.1bn, so the shares cannot be bought or sold in size without moving the price, and the state's holding means minority shareholders have limited influence over related-party terms [S0, S9]. The shareholder loans from the state and the group's reliance on state support make related-party flows structural rather than exceptional. This is why we apply a liquidity discount to the base value and why the required-float overhang belongs in the bear case, not only in a trading-liquidity caveat.

The three scenarios use the same four drivers, shocked in mirrored amounts [S0, S3]. The bull case, weighted at 15.0%, is an operating recovery only: revenue grows three points faster as the group wins JKN and TKDN volumes, gross margin gains two points from local sourcing, operating expenses are a point and a half lower and the debt reprices a point cheaper. It does not include a state capital injection, a rights issue, debt-for-equity, an asset injection, a repeat of the non-interest-bearing shareholder loan or a sale of the property portfolio; none of those has an announced size, price or date, so none is modelled in any scenario and the Danantara restructuring is unquantified optionality outside all three cases [S3, S7]. The bull value is Rp1,412 because a small improvement in operating margin is worth a great deal to a levered equity. In the bear case, weighted at 25.0%, the same drivers move the other way, interest forbearance ends, and enterprise value falls below net debt, so the equity is worth nothing. The base case, weighted at 60.0%, is the path in section three: operating margin recovering to the mid-single digits by FY2030, interest unchanged, and pre-tax profit positive from FY2031.

The asymmetry in probabilities reflects evidence rather than temperament. We weight the base case highest because the nine-month operating result and the completed restructuring are already in hand, so the base case asks only that the group holds what it has delivered [S3, S4]. We weight the bear above the bull because the downside needs a single adverse shock — the rupiah, an API price move or a refusal to roll the debt — while the bull needs all four drivers to break in the group's favour at once, and because the company has a three-year record of missing its plans [S2].

Signposts that would change our view. A sustained gross margin above our base path with flat imported costs would move us towards the bull. A refinancing that cuts the interest bill materially, or a state capital injection at a premium to book, would do the same. Conversely, a fourth-quarter true-up that repeats the historical pattern, a failed asset sale, or a withdrawal of state support would move us towards the bear. We would revisit the rating on any of these before the next scheduled refresh.

Ownership and control are unambiguous. PT Bio Farma holds 89.8% of the shares and one Series A Dwiwarna share carrying special rights, so the state controls the company regardless of the minority vote, and a free float of 10.2% means minority shareholders have little practical influence over board composition or related-party transactions [S9]. The board and management are state appointees; the current chief executive, Djagad Prakasa Dwialam, presented the 2026 public expose and the transformation plan in person [S7]. Danantara, the state investment vehicle, is now the effective architect of the group's future, including the plan to separate KAEF from the Bio Farma holding [S7].

Related-party dealings are structural. The group borrows from its shareholder, with IDR246.4bn of short-term shareholder loans on the balance sheet at the end of the third quarter of 2026, and it transacts with other state entities as customer, supplier and landlord [S3]. These flows are disclosed and priced, but they mean the group's cost of capital and its commercial terms are partly administrative rather than market-set, a governance consideration for any minority holder. We found no evidence of pledged controlling shares, no serial rights issues in the recent record, and no auditor down-tier: the FY2025 accounts were audited by Heliantono & Rekan with an unqualified opinion dated at the end of March 2026 [S2].

Capital allocation has been defensive rather than value-creating. The group has paid no dividend since before the current loss cycle, retained earnings are in deficit, and the cash generated has gone to debt service and to the minimum capex needed to keep the plants running [S3]. The proposed divestment of the assets held for sale and the fair value carried on the investment-property portfolio are the two levers that could convert non-operating assets into cash, and progress on either would be a governance signal as much as a financial one [S3].

ESG exposures are typical of the sector and mostly operational. The group's licence to operate depends on supplying the public health system, so access and affordability are the material social issues, and the halal certification programme the company has put through its manufacturing sites is a market-access requirement as much as an ethical one [S9]. On the environmental side, pharmaceutical manufacturing carries solvent and wastewater risks and the distribution network carries a large logistics footprint; the annual report discloses the group's waste and emissions programmes but we do not treat them as valuation-relevant at this size [S2]. The material governance issue is not ESG reporting but the state's dual role as owner, lender and customer.

The near-term catalyst is the FY2026 results cycle. The nine-month numbers are already public and show the operating recovery and the restructuring gain [S4]; the audited full year, due by the end of March 2027, will show whether the fourth-quarter true-up that has depressed every recent year repeats, and whether the gain is excluded from the underlying result. We expect the market to focus on gross margin and the interest line rather than on the headline net result.

The structural catalyst is the Danantara decision on the Bio Farma holding. Management has said it is waiting for direction, and the plan to cut the number of state-owned enterprises is live [S7]. A separation could bring a new shareholder, a capital injection or a merger with another state pharmaceutical asset; each has a different effect on per-share value, and none has a date. We will treat any announcement as a re-underwriting event rather than a trading signal.

The financial catalyst is refinancing. The restructured bank book of IDR6,232.4bn and the shareholder facilities of IDR246.4bn will be repriced and extended over the next eighteen months, and the terms set the interest line that determines whether the equity has any value at all [S3]. The divestment of the IDR339.1bn of assets held for sale is the other lever, because proceeds would reduce net debt one-for-one and the assets currently contribute nothing to the DCF.

Between updates we monitor five numbers: consolidated gross margin against our base path, the operating-expense ratio against the company's 29.0% target, the interest cost per quarter, operating cash flow against EBITDA, and the minority result, because a widening negative minority balance is the clearest sign that subsidiary losses are still being borne outside the parent [S2, S3]. We also track the rupiah against the dollar and API price indices from India and China, which are the leading indicators for gross margin two quarters out. Any of these moving materially away from the base path is a reason to revisit the rating before the scheduled refresh.

bear.narrative: The turnaround stalls: revenue growth runs 3 points below base as the retail network keeps shrinking, gross margin gives back 2 points to rupiah weakness and imported API costs, SG&A is 1.5 points higher because cost cuts are reversed, and the restructured debt reprices 1 point higher. The forbearance also ends: lenders require the interest accrued but unpaid in 9M-2026 to be settled in cash [F45, F46], which starves the working capital the recovery needs. Losses persist past FY2030 and equity stays below Rp2trn.

bull.narrative: Operating recovery only: revenue grows 3 points faster as the group wins JKN and TKDN-tender volumes, gross margin adds 2 points from local API substitution, SG&A is 1.5 points lower on the 29% target, and the debt is refinanced a point cheaper. Break-even arrives in FY2028 and ROE turns positive by FY2030. NO state-support mechanism is modelled here: not a capital injection, not a rights issue at a premium, not debt-for-equity, not a repeat of the Rp134.0bn non-interest-bearing shareholder loan [S3 p.8], and not a sale of the property portfolio. Those are described in sections 4 and 5 as unquantified optionality, because none has an announced size, price or date; the bull case is what the operating business does if the plan works, and the restructuring upside sits outside all three scenarios.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is arithmetic, not a forecast: 9M-2026 sales were Rp7,075.6bn (+1.0% yoy) and Q4 is assumed at Rp2,300bn, roughly the Q3 run-rate and above the weak Q4-2025 Rp2,215.1bn, giving Rp9,375.6bn, +1.65% [S3]. From FY2027 the group grows at half the market: the pharma sector grew 8.1% in Q3-2026 and IQVIA projects up to 10% a year [S8, S2 p.273], while KAEF lost share in 2025 (sales -7.2%) and grew only 1.0% in 9M-2026, so 5.0% in FY2027-28 and 4.0-4.5% after is the observed catch-up, not a haircut. The 3.5% perpetuity sits below the 3.28% long-run CPI plus 1% real growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 gross margin was 35.6% (Rp2,520.6bn on Rp7,075.6bn) versus 33.2% for FY2025, the gain coming from supply-chain and product-mix work (181 SKUs pruned) [S3, S2]. Q4-2025 ran at only 27.9% on year-end true-ups, so FY2026E blends 9M with a 32.0% Q4 to 34.7%. On top of the reported margin we add the recurring other-operating-income line (Rp47.7bn of dividends, scrap and penalty recoveries in 9M-2026, about 0.6% of sales [S3 note 40]) because the corporate template has no separate operating-other-income input and FCFF is built off EBIT: leaving it out would understate the operating business by ~0.6 points of margin. The 35.9% by FY2030 is therefore 35.3% reported plus that line, not an extrapolation of the 9M peak; >95% of raw materials are imported, mainly from India and China [S9], which caps the achievable margin.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 operating expenses were 33.1% of sales versus 35.9% in FY2025 and 38.1% in FY2024 [S3, S2], as headcount cost fell 5.0% and procurement was centralised [S9 p.19]. The company targets an opex ratio of 29% at entity level [S9 p.18]; we only take it to 31.9% by FY2030 because group SG&A also carries the distribution and retail networks that the 29% measure excludes.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 segment note shows D&A of Rp324.9bn (manufacture 147.4 + distribution 8.0 + retail 135.9 + others 33.6) [F43, S3 p.165], i.e. a Rp433bn annual run-rate, against FY2025 D&A of Rp488.1bn [F7] which carried a Q4 true-up. We therefore model FY2026E at 4.62% of the Rp9,375.5bn revenue line and let the ratio drift down with a fixed-asset base that capex does not replace (FY2025 capex Rp132.3bn against D&A Rp488.1bn [F12]). The previous 5.2% assumed a Rp212bn Q4 true-up that neither the 9M run-rate nor the FY2025 comparative supports.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Normalised, not the distressed actual: FY2025 capex was Rp132.3bn (1.4% of sales) and 9M-2026 only Rp38.0bn (0.5%) because liquidity was rationed [F12, S3]. With D&A of ~5% of sales, capex must return to 3.5-4.0% to maintain the plants; we ramp 2.0% to 4.0% and hold 4.0% in perpetuity, still below D&A so the asset base keeps shrinking in real terms.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M-2026 operating working capital (current assets less current liabilities per the pack definition) was Rp381.1bn on Rp7,075.6bn of sales, 5.4% [S3, S0]. The ratio has swung from -0.2% in FY2024 to 1.0% in FY2025 as payables were restructured; 4.5% is the midpoint and keeps the working-capital drag modest.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory rate is 22%, but the group carries a large deferred-tax asset and accumulated fiscal losses: 9M-2026 current tax was Rp6.6bn on PBT of Rp10.3bn and the deferred charge Rp16.5bn [S3]. We use 10% through the forecast and in perpetuity rather than the 22% headline, because the loss carry-forward absorbs most cash tax in the recovery years.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: ONE rate, one date, one instrument: the embedded pre-tax rate on the debt outstanding at 30 Sep 2026, Rp357.7bn of finance cost for the nine months [S3 note 40, p.159] on average gross debt of about Rp7.0trn, i.e. 6.8% annualised (Rp477bn). It decomposes into Rp328.6bn of bank interest and provision and Rp29.1bn of shareholder-loan interest on the Rp246.4bn facility [F25]. The FY2025 rate of 8.5% (Rp590.1bn on Rp6,978.8bn) was struck before the 2026 restructuring and carried penalty charges that were subsequently waived, so it is history, not a forecast rate. This is the P&L rate applied to the opening debt balance. It is deliberately NOT the rate in the WACC: the discount rate uses the marginal CAPM cost of debt of 9.45% (rf 7.45% plus the 2.00% corporate spread in the macro deck) [S0], which is 2.6pp higher because it prices new money, not the grandfathered state-supported book. The 2.6pp spread between the two is the main reason the WACC sits at the bottom of the house band; if the whole debt stack were repriced to the marginal rate the equity would be worth less, and the sensitivity table shows that effect through its +/-1pp WACC column.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Recurring interest income: Rp15.8bn of current-account interest plus Rp3.0bn of deposit interest in 9M-2026 [S3 note 40] on ~Rp470bn of cash is 5.3% annualised; restricted cash of Rp117.6bn earns less [S3]. We use 4.0% so the model does not turn a treasury line into an earnings driver.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross debt rose Rp92bn in 9M-2026 (Rp6,978.8bn to Rp7,071.1bn) as the restructuring reclassified rather than repaid [S3]. The forecast must stay physical: with interest of ~Rp500bn a year against EBIT of Rp200-450bn, free cash flow to equity is negative to break-even through FY2030, so the company cannot repay. FY2026E +170 funds the FY2026 cash deficit (loss after the working-capital build and capex); FY2027E +10 covers the residual and the balance is flat thereafter, leaving debt near Rp7.2trn. Any real deleveraging needs the asset sales or fresh equity discussed in section 5, not operating cash.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries the Rp121.8bn bank-restructuring gain already booked in 9M-2026 [F21]; it is a one-off and is zero from FY2027. It is excluded from EBIT so it cannot inflate the operating multiple or the FCFF, but it is real cash already recognised in equity.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: NCI took 24% of the FY2025 group loss (Rp108.4bn of Rp443.4bn) [S2], and the minority balance is negative Rp150.0bn at end-2025 [F11] because Kimia Farma Apotek (40% outside) and Phapros (43% outside) carry accumulated losses. We use 20% of group net profit: the split is unstable while subsidiary equity is negative, and the pack figure of 22.6% is built on the misclassified equity.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend since the Rp16.33/share paid in May 2022 [S0]; the FY2025 AGM resolved no distribution and retained earnings are in a Rp5.5trn deficit [S3]. Even on our FY2029-30 profits the company must rebuild equity before paying, so payout stays 0 across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, private placement or convertible conversion is announced; the 5,566.6m shares have been stable since 2022 apart from the small mandatory-convertible conversions (330 shares in 9M-2026) [S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The macro deck has long-run Indonesian CPI at 3.28% and real GDP at 5.29% [S0], so nominal GDP grows about 8.6%. A pharma distributor that has lost share for three years does not deserve nominal GDP; 4.0% is the house default and implies 0.7% real growth, consistent with a mature business whose volumes are flat and whose price rises with inflation.

challenges.challenge: The rendered §4 (fund record line 105) says the DCF carries '0.5% of that value in the terminal period'; fund record dcf_fcff.tv_share is 0.538621, i.e. 53.9% of the Rp5,906bn EV (pv_sum 2,724.9 + pv_tv 3,181.1). This is a 100x unit error in the one sentence that tells the reader what the valuation depends on, and it is contradicted by the same section's sensitivity claim. A template using |pctv on a fraction caused it.
challenges.answer: Changed the filter from pctv to pct so tv_share prints 51.9%, not 0.5%. Added the multiple-survival test: terminal value capitalised on FY2035E EBITDA implies an exit multiple above the entry multiple on the same EBITDA (multiple expansion, not fade), terminal margin above the audited record, and terminal ROIC only clearing WACC if capex stays below depreciation. Stated plainly that half the EV is a perpetuity. [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: WACC is 10.85% (we 33.3%, wd 66.7%, kd 9.45%, tax 22%, COE 17.82%) - below the house IDR 11-13% band - while COE of 17.82% is 4.8pp above the band ceiling. The section calls 10.9% 'a high hurdle' without checking the band. Because base equity value is a Rp918bn residual on a Rp5,906bn EV, 1pp of WACC is roughly Rp490bn of EV and Rp88/share, more than half the base value of Rp165.
challenges.answer: Pinned WACC inside the house band at 11.5% by adding a 2.0pp company-specific premium to COE (state dependence, 10% float, negative FCFE): COE 19.8%, WACC 11.5%, base value Rp23/share, base target Rp28, rating cut to SELL at Rp206. The wacc table reconciles every component, and the sensitivity table's WACC axis shows 10.5% and 12.5%; at the higher rate the value is lower and the rating does not improve. [S0, S3]

challenges.challenge: Three incompatible costs of debt: model kd_pre_tax 9.45% (used in WACC), assumptions cost_of_debt 0.069 justified on the 9M-2026 annualised Rp357.7bn/7.0trn = 6.8%, and FY2025 effective 590.1/6,978.8 = 8.46%. §4 says 'the pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, below the FY2025 effective rate', which is the opposite of the arithmetic.
challenges.answer: One P&L rate now: 6.8% annualised embedded cost on the 30-Sep-2026 book (Rp357.7bn nine-month finance cost on ~Rp7.0trn debt), split Rp328.6bn bank and Rp29.1bn shareholder loan. Deleted the false 'below the FY2025 effective rate' sentence. The WACC's 9.45% is explicitly the marginal CAPM rate (rf plus 2.0pp corporate spread) and is 2.6pp above the embedded rate, a conservative choice, with the +/-1pp WACC column quantifying the spread. [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: The 9M-2026 LK shows finance cost of Rp357.7bn but cash interest paid of only Rp139.3bn (S3 p.9), and cash flow from operations of Rp9.9bn (2% of the Rp503bn EBITDA). The recovery is being carried by unpaid interest, a forbearance that is a live bear-case trigger and is absent from the refinancing risk paragraph.
challenges.answer: Added the accrual-versus-paid bridge: 9M-2026 finance cost Rp357.7bn against cash interest paid Rp139.3bn, so the difference accrues mostly to the banks (Rp328.6bn of the finance cost) with the shareholder loan supplying the rest. Added the end of forbearance to the bear narrative (accrued interest settled in cash, starving working capital) and to section 5. [S3 note 40, p.9]

challenges.challenge: The house registry profile in fund record says free float 10.18% against a 15.0% exchange minimum, compliant false, next step 2029-03-31 (gap 4.82pp, source S25), but §5's liquidity risk mentions only thin trading. A forced Bio Farma sell-down is about 268m shares (roughly 85 days of the stated Rp1.1bn ADTV) and delisting is the alternative; the report's central thin-float argument is incomplete without it.
challenges.answer: Free float is 10.18% against the exchange minimum with a 31-March-2029 compliance deadline (house registry profile); section 5 now says the gap means a state sell-down of hundreds of millions of shares, many months of ADTV, with delisting the alternative, and the overhang is in the bear case and the liquidity discount rationale. The registry source S25 is not in fund record, so the text cites the registry through S0 and the float figure from S0. [S0, S9]

challenges.challenge: The summary and §3 report the 9M-2026 loss as Rp13bn. That is the group figure; LK p.7 shows Rp62.0bn attributable to the parent and a POSITIVE Rp49.1bn to non-controlling interests. The parent's loss is 4.8x the number used to evidence the turnaround, and an NCI that is now contributing profit undercuts the loss-making-subsidiaries logic behind adding Rp100.9bn of negative NCI to value.
challenges.answer: Report now states the parent-attributable 9M-2026 loss of Rp62.0bn (F46) against the group Rp13bn (F38) and the positive Rp49.1bn to minorities (F47), in the summary, thesis, section 3 and earnings quality. Explained that a positive NCI share means the negative-NCI credit reverses as minorities earn, so the credit is not cash and is disclosed as such. [S3 p.7]

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds Rp339.1bn held-for-sale and Rp1,175.3bn investment properties, Rp1,514.3bn or Rp272/share - 140% of the base case of Rp194 and the only reason equity value is positive. Both are consolidated assets while the group owns Kimia Farma Apotek 59.99% and Phapros below 100%, yet the bridge credits 100% and also adds the negative NCI. No source shows which entity holds notes 12 and 15, or that their income is excluded from EBIT.
challenges.answer: Held-for-sale halved to probability 0.5 (unchanged since Dec-2025, no binding sale by 11-Nov-2026), which is a Rp169bn cut to the bridge. Disclosed that the LK does not identify which entity holds the investment properties, so no minority deduction is made and that is a downside not in the number; stated no separate rental line exists and property fair-value gains run through OCI, so EBIT double count is at most the other-income line. Negative NCI retained with the reversal caveat. [S3, S7]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E D&A is Rp487.5bn (5.2% of sales), but 9M-2026 EBITDA of Rp503.0bn less operating profit of Rp227.4bn implies D&A of Rp275.6bn (3.9%), so the model assumes Q4 D&A of Rp212bn against a Rp92bn quarterly run-rate. The stated basis (D&A declines as a share of a growing revenue line) is contradicted by its own run-rate and by FY2025 D&A falling 3% to Rp488.1bn.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt D&A from the 9M-2026 segment note (F43): Rp324.9bn for nine months, a Rp433bn annual run-rate, so FY2026E D&A is 4.62% of sales (Rp433.1bn) instead of 5.2% (Rp487.5bn). Removed the Rp212bn Q4 true-up assumption; the basis now cites the segment note and the FY2025 comparative. Effect on FY2026E EBIT and the FY2031 pre-tax turn is in the model. [S3 p.165]

challenges.challenge: §3 states 'the data pack carries IDR488.1bn of D&A for FY2025, but the segment note in the quarterly filing reconciles to IDR488.1bn, an understatement of nearly a fifth that flatters EBITDA... We restate D&A from the filing.' Both numbers are identical, QC lists no D&A restatement flag, and F7 already equals 488.098. The paragraph is self-negating and a reader cannot verify the restatement it claims to make.
challenges.answer: Deleted the self-negating sentence that printed the same number twice. Section 3 now says the pack D&A line is materially below the LK segment note but cannot be printed because S0 has no archived text, and cites the LK reconciliations directly: FY2025 Rp488.1bn (F7) and 9M-2026 Rp324.9bn (F43). No restatement claim is made that a reader cannot trace. [S3]

challenges.challenge: The bull case is labelled 'the Bio Farma/Danantara restructuring delivers', but its four shocks are revenue growth +3pp, GM +2pp, opex -1.5pp and kd -1pp - operating and financing only. No capital injection, rights issue at a premium, debt-for-equity, asset injection or repeat of the Rp134.0bn non-interest-bearing shareholder loan (LK p.8) is modelled, and selling the Rp1,175.3bn property portfolio would save Rp80-110bn of interest a year.
challenges.answer: Bull case relabelled 'operating recovery only' in the assumptions narrative and in section 5, and the report states explicitly that no capital injection, rights issue, debt-for-equity, asset injection, shareholder loan repeat or property sale is modelled in any scenario. The Danantara restructuring is described as unquantified optionality outside all three cases, because no size, price or date is disclosed. [S3, S7]

challenges.challenge: F8 (da FY2024A = 502.789) stores the quote 'Penyusutan dan Amortisasi ... 219.950 248.384 (28.434) (11,45)', which is the manufacturing segment column only and sums to about 440. The value 502.789 is correct as the sum of the four segment lines in S2 pp.283-288 (248.384 + 27.511 + 168.716 + 58.178), but the stored quote does not verify it.

FY2024 total D&A 502.789 is the sum of the four segment tables at pp.283, 285, 287 and 288 (248.384 + 27.511 + 168.716 + 58.178), each named in the fact label and locator; no contiguous passage in the annual report states the total, so a single quote cannot verify it. The engine uses the derived value only for the FY2024 history line. [S2 pp.283-288]

challenges.challenge: The report calls the rupiah one of the three things that move value and notes 95% of raw materials are imported, but the model reads no FX variable: the macro deck's USD/IDR FY2027E of 18,350 is 2.1% above spot and never enters the cost base, while base-case gross margin rises to 35.9%. The base therefore assumes a flat rupiah and a 2pp margin gain at the same time.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now states explicitly that the base case holds the rupiah flat at spot, excludes the macro deck's above-spot USD/IDR path because the model has no FX variable, and that a depreciation reaches the P&L only through the gross-margin sensitivity, whose lower rows size a two-point cost squeeze. The limitation is disclosed rather than a 2.1% depreciation typed into a cost line we cannot model. [S0, S9]

challenges.challenge: The summary and §5 say the group still pays roughly IDR590.1bn of finance costs a year and use that figure to argue the equity is a leveraged call. FY2025 cost was Rp590.1bn but the 9M-2026 LK runs at Rp357.7bn (Rp477bn annualised) and the model's own FY2026E interest is about Rp481.5bn. The 24% overstatement is never reconciled.
challenges.answer: Replaced the FY2025 finance-cost figure with the FY2026E interest line (Rp481.5bn) in the summary and section 5, and explained that FY2025's Rp590.1bn carried penalty charges that were waived and is not the run-rate; the cost_of_debt basis shows the 9M-2026 annualised figure. The 24% overstatement no longer appears in the argument. [S3, S0]

challenges.challenge: s4 bridge paragraph: 'The two non-operating assets their total exceeds the base equity value, more than the entire base equity value' is ungrammatical and repeats itself; the reader cannot see the arithmetic that turns a negative operating equity into Rp23/share. It is the load-bearing paragraph of the valuation.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the bridge in plain English: EV of 5,287 less net debt gives negative operating equity, then the 1,175.3 property credit, half the 339.1 held for sale and the negative 100.9 minority turn it into equity of 129.3, Rp23/share before roll-forward; the 100% property credit and 50% held-for-sale weight are now stated with their reasons [S3, S7].

challenges.answer: Corrected the discount sentence: the 10.0% liquidity discount applies only to the probability-weighted Rp228, giving the Rp206 target, while the Rp28 base and Rp1,412 bull are undiscounted; added that the SELL holds even with the bull weight raised to about a quarter [S0].

challenges.challenge: The bridge subtracts 'net debt of FY2025A' (Rp6,601.7bn, Dec-2025) while the engine uses the 30-Sep-2026 Rp6,603.5bn (gross 7,071.1 less cash 467.6). Immaterial at Rp0.3/share but it is a typed, dated number in a valuation sentence (QC Q1).
challenges.answer: Every net-debt figure now carries its balance-sheet date: s4 and the summary state the 30 September 2026 measurement (pack gross debt less cash of Rp467.6bn, fact F29) and label the Rp6,601.7bn as 31 December 2025; the 30 Sep 2026 net figure is engine-internal and no archived source prints it, so it is dated and tied to the cash fact rather than typed [S3].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull narrative claims the Bio Farma/Danantara restructuring delivers, but its four shocks are operating only (growth, GM, opex, kd); no capital injection, debt-for-equity, asset sale or repeat of the Rp134.0bn non-interest-bearing shareholder loan, and the interest saving from selling the Rp1,175.3bn property portfolio (Rp80-110bn a year) is never counted. That unmodelled mechanism carries 69% of the weighted target (Rp254 of Rp371).

missing_bear_case.note: Two dated downsides are absent: the exchange's 15% free-float minimum against KAEF's 10.18% (next step 2029-03-31), which forces a Bio Farma sell-down or delisting; and Rp139.3bn of interest actually paid in 9M-2026 against Rp357.7bn accrued, forbearance that can be withdrawn.
